596.s: Powell thanks Rowe for the documentation, then talks about Joe Williams, his biography, and a week as guest at the Rainbow Room.

617.t: The element of surprise and Joe Williams
617.s: Predictable head-solos-fours format puts audiences to sleep; composition and surprise, recalled with Matt Wilson and Joe Williams.
617.q: Right. Exactly. And the element of surprise. Matt Wilson had a wonderful workshop yesterday and I advocated also, we have such history now of playing music that is jazz, and we play the head. And then we take solos. And then we take fours. And then the drums do this. So now everybody does it that…

557.t: Joe Williams and the blues as the basis of jazz
557.s: Roker says Williams can really sing the blues, and explains jazz as rooted in blues and Gospel feeling, including a happy kind of blues.
557.q: Because he can really sing the blues. And if you play jazz, if it doesn’t feel like the blues is involved, then it’s classical. You know what I’m saying? Jazz, the basics of jazz is the blues.

450.t: Joe Williams and the Basie band recording
450.s: Joe Williams sang the melody and they rehearsed under a Philadelphia stage before performing with the Basie band; she mentions skipping two octaves on 'Airegin'.
450.q: I remember rehearsing under the stage of the theater, I think it was in Philly. And we rehearsed down there and then we went up and did it because it was with the Basie band.

549.t: Joe Williams and meeting Jo Jones
549.s: At Randall's Island, his mother's remark leads Jo Jones to adopt Phil as a babysitter.
549.q: Well he was the reason why I met Jo Jones. When we were at the Randall’s Island Festival in 1956 and Count Basie band was plenty hot and they had “Everyday I Have the Blues” which was a hit single, and the album “April in Paris,” which I believe had come out as a big selling record, and my mother…

423.t: Playing behind Joe Williams on the Tonight Show
423.s: He often accompanied Joe Williams, a popular guest on Carson's show, and is fond of him.
423.q: I played behind Joe a great deal on the Tonight Show. Not with the Basie band because he wasn’t with the Basie band at that time. But I played for Joe a lot. Because he was a very popular guest on the Carson show. I think, if you ask Joe, I don’t think it’s an © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

358.t: Joe Williams in Club DeLisa and the Buffalo false start
358.s: He recalls Joe singing Pagliacci in a show, then a first gig with Joe in Buffalo while with Carmen McRae, which went badly.
358.q: Singing Pagliacci in the Club DeLisa and doing a show. And that’s how broad the shows were, the kind of shows they presented. They really, it wasn’t just about jumping up and down, I mean there was a format to what they were doing. Very organized.

424.s: Smith describes Joe Williams's tenor-like timbre and melodic phrasing.
424.q: Well, on the same stage. I haven’t—because he’s usually had Norman Simmons playing for him, even if I’m the studio pianist in the orchestra, you know, he’s got his own piano player. But I’ve known Joe all these years, and always been a fan of his.

361.t: Joe Williams and Sweets Edison's band; never playing Rochester
361.s: Playing behind Joe Williams in Edison's group, which later played his hometown.
361.q: Oh it was great. I worked with Sweets Edison, he had a group behind Joe Williams. We worked out here in different places. I took Tommy Flanagan’s place on that particular

219.s: Wein calls Joe Williams a great ballad and jazz-blues singer, remembering him arriving at Storyville with Basie.
219.q: Joe Williams was a great singer. Everybody thought he was a blues singer. Well put it this way, Joe Williams could sing the blues. But he was a great ballad singer. And that’s, I think in his heart he wanted to be a ballad singer. But he sang the blues as well as anybody. Big band jazz blues. He…

944.t: Joe Williams and the year with Basie
944.s: A year of festivals with Basie and Joe Williams, leaving over low pay; Williams helped start the archive.
944.q: Yeah. Well I appreciate you for asking me all these questions you know. And I see that you’ve got Joe Williams on your wall there.

108.t: Short time with Basie and Joe Williams as a ballad singer
108.s: He was with Basie far less than a year; he knew Joe Williams as a ballad singer in Hampton's band and was surprised by his blues success.
108.q: No, Joe wasn’t on the band at that time. I met Joe Williams, incidentally the first time I worked with Joe Williams, he was the vocalist with Lionel Hampton’s band. He sang in Lionel Hampton’s band. No blues, he was a ballad singer, and a good one. He sang ballads, beautiful singer. And when he…

679.t: Joe Williams on film and his present stage persona
679.s: Wolff is a fan of Joe Williams, collects his films including early Basie clips, and says he is now comfortable and happy.
679.q: I have a wonderful — I’m a particular fan of Joe’s, both professionally and personally. I’ve seen him so many times in recent years, particularly on the jazz cruises, one of his favorite places to perform. So I’ve been a collector of Joe Williams for some time, and I think I have a pretty wide…

61.t: Joe Williams: the consummate professional at RCA and Newport
61.s: Studio dates with Jimmy Jones and the Newport album; Anderson danced in the aisles.
61.ch: RCA years: Rollins, Nero and singers
61.q: Joe, I felt, is the greatest male singer of all time, after Louis Armstrong. I always have to put Louis first, because he’s in a class by himself. He’s the daddy, like Billie Holiday. “I’m as close as I can get to Louis Armstrong,” she would say. Joe was the absolute professional all the way. It…

369.t: Joe Williams next door selling newspapers
369.s: Joe Williams lived in the next building and remembered her practicing constantly when she was twelve or thirteen.
369.ch: Family roots, South Side and early training
369.q: Joe Williams said that’s all I did. Joe Williams lived in the next building, you know. And he would sell newspapers on the corner.

73.s: Greene recalls Joe Williams as an usher he'd forgotten and how the hit saved the band.
73.ch: Small group, new sound and Europe
73.q: Yes. But, as I say, he made me remember -- and I had forgotten that he had worked at the -- you know -- he used to say -- "You know, I used to be an usher at the --". And, I remember seeing him after, you know, he told me that.

86.t: Ernie Wilkins and Joe Williams' Every Day revive Basie
86.s: They sort out who arranged Every Day and credit Wilkins and Joe Williams for Basie's popularity returning.
86.q: Yeah, sure. And then Ernie Wilkins did (HUMMING) -- oh, I can't think of it.* We played it last night. He did that and, oh, he did such fantastic -- Ernie did a lot of --
